newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajikistan fears spread of Afghan fighting.
newsitem.headline: Tajikistan fears spread of Afghan fighting.

text.p: Security officials in Tajikistan held an emergency meeting on Tuesday, fearing fresh fighting in Afghanistan could spread to their former Soviet republic or prompt a flood of refugees.
"The meeting was prompted by current events in Afghanistan," a senior army officer, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters.
"The two main issues on the agenda were the reinforcement of the Tajik-Afghan border and a possible massive influx of refugees from northern Afghanistan."

The meeting in Dushanbe took place a day after General Abdul Malik, a key commander under northern opposition leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum, launched a mutiny and went over to the Islamic Taleban militia, which controls most of the country.

The fear of Afghan fighting and hordes of refugees spilling into Tajikistan, already impoverished by its own civil war, has haunted Dushanbe since last September, when Taleban seized the Afghan capital Kabul.
The presence in Afghanistan of thousands of Tajik refugees and Tajik opposition fighters, who are now involved in peace talks with Dushanbe, complicates matters for the Tajik authorities.

During April's Taleban advance towards northern Afghanistan, controlled by Dostum, Russia and four Central Asian states -- Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan -- discussed how to keep the Afghan conflict away from their territories.
The five former Soviet republics agreed to rebuff any attempt by Taleban to spread the fighting onto their soil, but rejected proposals to offer outright help to Dostum, an ethnic Uzbek.

Russia stepped up the readiness of the 20,000 peacekeepers it has deployed in Tajikistan and the Russian frontier guards who help patrol the 1,387-km (867-mile) Tajik frontier with Afghanistan. But it decided against sending reinforcements.

Prior to Malik's defection, the Taleban already controlled two-thirds of Afghan territory. Taleban officials have issued enthusiastic reports on their military success against Dostum but no independent confirmation has been available.
Tajik President Imomali Rakhmonov said last month that up to a million refugees could pour into his impoverished country of 5.7 million in the event of fierce fighting in northern Afghanistan.
Rakhmonov said he was afraid that, together with refugees, armed bands of Islamist extremists could infiltrate Tajikistan.
The fear of militant Islam spreading into the region is a major factor of concern for Central Asian leaders.

"We do not rule out that the events in Afghanistan will affect Tajikistan," the senior Tajik army source said. "Over 1,000 refugees -- mostly ethnic Tajiks -- are crowded at one of the border checkpoints ready to flee to Tajikistan."
